lesson.title: Ask Python Directly: The type() Function
lesson.summary: The built-in type() function inspects a value and reports its exact type without modifying it, making it one of the fastest ways to confirm what a program actually produced.
lesson.body:
When you are not sure what type a value actually is, the most direct way to find out is to ask Python itself using the built-in type() function. Calling type(x) does not change x in any way; it simply inspects the value currently bound to x and returns an object describing its type, which Python displays in the form <class 'int'>, <class 'float'>, <class 'bool'>, or <class 'str'> for the types covered earlier in this unit. This function is one of the most useful debugging tools available, because a huge share of bugs in real code come down to a value having a type the programmer did not expect.

Here is a trace that shows type() in action across several values:

a = 7
b = 7.0
c = "7"
d = True
print(type(a))
print(type(b))
print(type(c))
print(type(d))

Even though a, b, and c all involve the digit 7 and might look similar at a glance, they print as <class 'int'>, <class 'float'>, and <class 'str'> respectively, because 7 is a whole number literal, 7.0 has a decimal point, and "7" is wrapped in quotes. The value d prints as <class 'bool'>, not <class 'int'>, even though bool is technically built on top of int, because type() reports the most specific type of the object, not a broader category it happens to also belong to.

type() is especially useful right after a calculation whose result type is not obvious just from reading the code. For example, dividing two integers with / always produces a float in Python, even when the division comes out even: type(10 / 2) reports <class 'float'>, not <class 'int'>, which surprises many beginners who expect whole number division to stay a whole number. Checking with type() in moments like this turns a guess into a verified fact instead.

type() is also commonly paired with the comparison operator == inside conditional logic, as in if type(value) == int:, to make a program branch differently depending on what kind of data it received. In most everyday code, the built-in function isinstance() is preferred for that particular job because it also accounts for subtypes correctly, but type() remains the clearest, most direct tool for simply asking, and immediately seeing, what type a given value is right now. That direct feedback is exactly what makes it worth reaching for constantly while learning, and later while debugging more complex programs.

isinstance() is worth introducing alongside type() specifically because of how it handles the bool and int relationship covered in the boolean type lesson. type(True) == int evaluates to False, since type() reports bool as the exact, most specific type, but isinstance(True, int) evaluates to True, because isinstance() correctly recognizes that bool counts as a kind of int even though it is not identical to it. Neither function is simply "better" than the other; type() answers the narrow question of exactly what a value is, while isinstance() answers the broader, and usually more useful, question of what category a value belongs to.
